certainty_reasoning: The evidence read so far is Wilde's own twelve letters to Dowson (the primary source for this pair) plus Dowson's own words about Wilde as printed by Frankel from the Flower-Maas edition - so both participants are on record, which is rare here. That clears the readme's bar twice over: the ardour is legible as ardour without the coding hypothesis, and a scholarly source reads it that way (McKenna: 'their friendship suddenly seemed to deepen into love'). Frankel - the specialist monograph for exactly these years, and the most recent scholarship in the corpus - reads it flatly as 'frank and unguarded friendship' and never suggests otherwise; Dowson's own surviving words about Wilde are admiring, wry and entirely non-romantic; Dowson's documented sexual interest was in women, and by both Sox's and Frankel's accounts he tried to steer Wilde toward women; and the ardent lines are a handful within a correspondence that is otherwise practical (poems, absinthe, a translation, a debt). Sox prints it in an agentless passive with an endnote (n. 12) that names no describer and merely cross-refers to Wilde's own 16 June letter, which does not contain it; the phrase appears nowhere in the Complete Letters, so it is not Wilde's; and McKenna, the only other corpus source to use it, cites Sox p. 141 for it, closing the loop.
date_label: Acquainted from 1890; Dowson visited Wilde at Oakley Street between the trials, spring 1895. The letters that carry the ardour are Berneval/Dieppe, June-August 1897, concentrated in the fortnight 16-30 June; Dowson returned to England in mid-July 1897. Four further letters from Naples, October 1897, are practical. Wilde's last word on Dowson is his letter of condolence to Smithers, circa 24 February 1900.
summary: Dowson met Wilde in 1890 through the London literary world and, with Robert Sherard, called on him at Oakley Street between the trials in 1895 - one of very few who did. In the summer of 1897 he was living at Arques-la-Bataille near Dieppe and became the closest daily companion of Wilde's first free months, dining at Berneval on 3 June and thereafter meeting almost constantly at the Cafe Suisse in Dieppe. Wilde's letters over the following fortnight turn markedly warm: he tells Dowson there is 'a fatality about our being together', asks why he is 'so persistently and perversely wonderful', watches for the green costume that suits his 'dark hyacinth locks', calls his absence the one imperfection in an otherwise perfect day, and signs himself 'Tout a toi'. Dowson's own letters of the same weeks are affectionate but unromantic - he found Wilde's 'enormous joy in life' hard to match - and he is reported to have tried to interest Wilde in women; Wilde later told Fothergill they had quarrelled and that Dowson had cut off his long curls to spite him. The friendship survived it in a lower key, and when Dowson died in February 1900 Wilde asked Smithers to lay flowers on his grave.

sources.quote: There is a fatality about our being together that is astounding – or rather quite probable. Had I stayed at Arques I should have given up all hopes of ever separating from you. Why are you so persistently and perversely wonderful? … I suppose I shall see you in ten minutes from this. I am looking out for the green costume that goes so well with your dark hyacinth locks. … Now I am alive, and all is perfect, except your absence. Tout à toi
sources.context: Wilde to Ernest Dowson, [? 16 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Maguire); signed sebastian melmoth. Elisions drop the servant anecdote, the paragraph on Thompson and Socrates, the line 'Come with vine-leaves in your hair' (the editors gloss it to Ibsen's Hedda Gabler), and the first half of the Pernod sentence. Full letter. 'Hyacinth' is Wilde's Douglas register: cf. Wilde to Douglas, 'Hyacinthus, whom Apollo loved so madly, was you in Greek days' (Complete Letters p. 544, cited at Frankel p. 328 n. 30).
sources.supports: Wilde's own most explicit statement of attachment to Dowson: inseparability, a compliment on Dowson's hair in the mythological register he used for Douglas, absence as the single flaw in the day, and 'Tout à toi'. This is also the letter Sox is quoting for both 'the green costume' and 'dark hyacinth locks'.
sources.provenance: PDF page 951, printed folio 901 confirmed on the rendered page. Three elisions marked with spaced ellipses; nothing omitted alters the sense of what is quoted. The editors reproduce a photograph of Dowson in the unfoliated plate section (PDF 600, plate 85) captioned with the first sentence of this passage.

sources.quote: My dear Ernest, Do come here at once: Monsieur Meyer is presiding over a morning meal of absinthe, and we want you. I am a wreck of course, but la belle soeur is like the moon. You were wonderful and charming all last night. Ever yours OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Ernest Dowson, [? 24 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Maguire) - the entire letter. Line breaks between the three sentences run together here.
sources.supports: The register at its warmest outside the 16 June letter, and the daily rhythm of the Dieppe weeks
sources.provenance: PDF page 957, printed folio 907 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Dear Ernest, I must see you: so I propose to breakfast at St Martin L'Eglise tomorrow at 11.30 and you must come: take a voiture and be there. I want to have a poet to talk to, as I have had lots of bad news since you left me. Do try, like a good chap, to be there, and wear a blue tie. I want to be consoled.
sources.context: Postcard, Wilde to Ernest Dowson, Monday [postmark 28 June 1897], [postmark Dieppe] (MS Maguire); signed sebastian melmoth. Italics on 'must', 'voiture' and 'blue' in the original. The 'bad news' is his solicitor's resignation and the cancellation of Douglas's visit (Frankel, p. 116).
sources.supports: Summons and dependence: Wilde asking to be consoled, and prescribing what Dowson is to wear - the second such instruction in a week
sources.provenance: PDF page 958, printed folio 908 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Dear Ernest, I write a little line, whose only excuse is its entire illegibility, to tell you how charming you are (at Berneval) and how much I like your friend, and mine, the dear Achille. … You and Achille and Achille's friend and I must all be at Berneval together. I am making arrangements. Give to Achille my sincere friendship: you have it, and other things, always.
sources.context: Wilde to Ernest Dowson, Wednesday 6.30 [? 30 June 1897], Café Suisse, Dieppe (MS Maguire); signed S. M. The letter runs over the printed 908/909 page break. 'Achille' is glossed by the editors as presumably Achille Fromentin. The elision drops the paragraph praising Dowson's 'lovely lyrics' and a passage about a costermonger. The closing clause is addressed to Dowson though its sentence is nominally about Achille.
sources.supports: The only line in the twelve letters that gestures at something withheld from the page ('and other things, always'), and the plan to gather the four of them at Berneval
sources.provenance: PDF pages 958-959, printed folios 908 and 909 both confirmed on the rendered pages. One elision marked with a spaced ellipsis; full letter.

sources.quote: Dowson was described as Wilde's 'first hyacinth since Douglas: But this flower was wilting, and had not much longer to live'. Despite the wilting, Wilde looked for 'the green costume' which went well with Dowson's 'dark hyacinth locks'. Fothergill commented that Dowson was in love with the owner of the Café Royal, but was 'faithful only after his fashion'. Although Dowson was in the house he did not appear. Wilde said they had quarrelled and Dowson, to spite him, 'had had all his long curls cut'.
sources.context: Sox, in the chapter 'Two Loves Have I', on the guests at Wilde's Chalet Bourgeat during Fothergill's own stay - 'Of the other guests at Chalet Bourgeat at this time, Fothergill mentioned seeing only two: Leonard Smithers … [and] the English poet Ernest Dowson' (p. 140). Sox's Part V note-head states that unnoted quotations in the section are from Fothergill's unpublished memoir, so the chain for the quarrel and the cut curls is Wilde -> Fothergill's memoir -> Sox. Endnote markers (nn. 12-13) omitted. Caution, and the reason this quote sits fifth rather than first: the 'first hyacinth' phrase is unattributed. Sox's n. 12 (printed p. 271) reads only 'Also see Hart-Davis, Selected Letters, pp. 290-1' - a cross-reference to Wilde's own 16 June letter, which does not contain the phrase. It is not Wilde's; McKenna, the only other corpus source to use it, cites Sox p. 141 for it. Whose words they are is a live open question. Note too the chronology tension: the Letters editors have Dowson back in England from mid-July (p. 924 n. 1), while Fothergill's undated visit falls in Wilde's last month at Berneval.
sources.supports: The only romantic characterization of the pair in the literature, and its unresolved attribution; Fothergill's counter-observation that Dowson's own attachment lay elsewhere; and the quarrel in which Dowson cut off the curls Wilde had admired - the evidential basis for outcome 'unreciprocated'
sources.provenance: PDF page 157, printed folio 141 confirmed on the rendered page; the setting sentence from PDF 156, printed folio 140 confirmed. Endnote 12 read on the rendered page at PDF 303, printed folio 271 confirmed, and the superscript markers on p. 141 checked in a 4x zoom render. Sox's index (printed p. 282) lists Dowson at p. 141 only, and a full-text search of the file confirms this is his sole treatment.

sources.quote: For his part, Dowson was impressed by Wilde's "enormous joy in life just at this moment" and "had some difficulty in suppressing my own sourness" as a result. His first impression was that Wilde had changed a great deal for the better: "he seems of much broader sympathies, much more human and simple. His delight in the country, in walking, in the simplicities of life is enchanting." … "His gorgeous spirits cheered me mightily," Dowson wrote of Wilde at this time
sources.context: Frankel quoting Dowson's own letters of summer 1897, from Letters of Ernest Dowson, ed. desmond Flower and Henry Maas (Fairleigh Dickinson up, 1968), pp. 384 and 387 - his notes 64, 65 and 68 at printed pp. 324-325. The elision drops Frankel's intervening paragraph on the brothel story and the absinthe. Frankel's own reading of the pair, on the same page and the one before, is 'frank and unguarded friendship' and Dowson as 'one of his closest confidantes' (p. 113).
sources.supports: The second participant's own testimony - the counter-weight that keeps this edge below a relationship class. Dowson's register toward Wilde is admiring and wry, never romantic.
sources.provenance: PDF page 128, printed folio 114 confirmed on the rendered page. Frankel's printed-to-PDF offset established so far as a constant PDF - 14, holding across body and notes. Frankel p. 113 read at PDF 127, folio confirmed. One elision marked with a spaced ellipsis; Frankel's own internal ellipsis inside the Dowson quotation is his.

sources.quote: They met frequently, and their friendship suddenly seemed to deepen into love. It is unlikely that the relationship was ever sexual, but there may have been drunken embraces and declarations of undying love.
sources.context: McKenna on the June 1897 Dieppe weeks, immediately before he quotes the 'fatality about our being together' letter. This is the one scholarly reading in the corpus that names the connection as love, and it is explicitly speculative ('seemed', 'may have been'); works.json records that McKenna is never a sufficient basis on his own. The file carries no printed folios, so the locator is a PDF page.
sources.supports: The scholarly-reading half of the readme's attraction-expressed bar - and, by its own hedging, the reason the class stays at attraction-expressed rather than rising higher
sources.provenance: PDF page 665; no printed folio or running head appears on the rendered page, consistent with the pagination warning on mckenna-2008 in works.json. McKenna's source note for the adjoining 'first hyacinth since Douglas' phrase, at PDF 852, reads 'Sox, Bachelors of Art, page 141'.

sources.quote: My dear Smithers, I am greatly distressed to hear of Ernest's death: how sudden it must have been! Poor wounded wonderful fellow that he was, a tragic reproduction of all tragic poetry, like a symbol, or a scene. I hope bay-leaves will be laid on his tomb, and rue, and myrtle too, for he knew what love is. He was a sweet singer … If he is not yet laid to rest or unrest, do put some flowers for me on his grave.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [circa 24 February 1900], Paris - written the day after Dowson died, and Wilde's last word on him. Addressed to a third party, so it is Wilde's own testimony but not part of the correspondence between the two men. The elision drops the simile comparing Dowson's note to birdsong in Shakespeare's day. The editors' footnote on the same page gives the death and burial particulars.
sources.supports: The close of the connection in Wilde's own voice; 'he knew what love is' is elegiac and unspecific - Wilde does not say for whom
sources.provenance: PDF page 1219, printed folio 1173 confirmed on the rendered page. One elision marked with a spaced ellipsis; full passage.
